  untouched), while adding migration risk and operational complexity to
  a workload that was never broken.
lessons.explanation:
**The mistake the junior engineer's "add more NameNode memory" proposal made was treating the symptom (memory pressure) as the problem, rather than diagnosing which specific workload characteristic was driving it -- and the platform team's fix worked because it correctly separated "HDFS has a small-file problem" from "HDFS is broadly inadequate for this cluster."**

**Why file count, not byte volume, is what stresses a NameNode:** HDFS keeps its entire namespace -- every file's metadata, every directory, every block-to-datanode mapping -- resident in the active NameNode's memory, because every metadata operation (a file open, a listing, a block lookup) has to be served from RAM to meet HDFS's latency expectations. This means the NameNode's memory footprint scales with the *number* of files and blocks, almost independent of their size. A single 500GB file split into a handful of 128MB-or-larger blocks costs the NameNode a small, roughly constant amount of metadata. A million 100KB files cost the NameNode a million times that overhead, while occupying a small fraction of the actual disk space the 500GB file does. This is exactly the mismatch in the scenario: millions of small risk-model files were the entire source of the NameNode pressure, while the enormous but few-in-number ledger extracts were essentially free from the NameNode's point of view.

**Why Ozone fixes specifically this problem, architecturally, not just "because it's newer":** Ozone does not use a single NameNode-style namespace holder at all. It is built as a distributed key-value/object store: Ozone Managers (which can themselves be scaled/replicated) track key-to-container metadata in RocksDB, and actual data lives in Storage Container Manager-managed containers, addressed directly rather than through one process's in-memory namespace tree. This is the concrete mechanism behind Ozone's suitability for very high object counts -- it was designed, from the ground up, around the assumption that metadata volume needs to scale independently of any single node's memory, which is precisely the axis HDFS's architecture does not scale well on.

**Why migrating only the small-file workload -- not the whole cluster -- was the right scope, and why moving the large files instead would have been a real mistake:** HDFS's block-oriented, POSIX-like design is still a good fit for large, sequentially-accessed files; nothing about the ledger extracts' access pattern (nightly batch write, repeated large sequential reads by Spark) benefits from Ozone's object-store semantics, and migrating them would have added real operational risk (a data-migration project, new access-pattern validation, retraining any tooling that assumed classic HDFS paths) for a workload that was never contributing to the actual problem. Meanwhile, if the team had "fixed" the NameNode pressure by moving the large files instead of the small ones, the true cause -- millions of small-file inodes still resident in NameNode memory -- would have remained completely untouched, and the pressure would have continued exactly as before.

**The general diagnostic principle this generalizes to:** before choosing a storage-layer migration, identify the specific resource being exhausted (here: NameNode metadata memory, which scales with file count) and the specific workload driving it (here: the small-file writer, not the large-file writer) -- then move only that workload to the architecture that actually addresses that specific bottleneck, rather than treating a platform-level migration as a blanket upgrade applied uniformly.
lessons.readinessNote: This lesson's HDFS-vs-Ozone distinction -- large sequential files staying well-served by HDFS, high-cardinality small objects moving to Ozone's distributed metadata model -- is the storage-layer foundation T02 (Hive/Impala/metastore), T04 (CDP architecture, SDX) and T05 (Iceberg) all build on: every later lesson in this chapter assumes the learner knows which storage layer a given table or object actually lives on, and why.

lessons.title: Hive and Impala
lessons.scenario: A transaction-monitoring team runs two kinds of queries against the same Iceberg tables on CDP: a nightly batch job that joins five years of transaction history against a slowly-changing customer dimension to rebuild a compliance report (runs for 40 minutes, touches nearly the whole table, tolerant of that latency), and an ad-hoc compliance-analyst workload where analysts run dozens of small, filtered lookups per day ('show me this one customer's transactions from last week') and expect sub-5-second responses. A new engineer, seeing both workloads hit the same tables, configures both to run through Hive, reasoning that 'one engine, one configuration, is simpler to operate.' The analysts' ad-hoc queries become the team's top complaint within a week -- each one taking 20-40 seconds even for a single customer's single week of data.
lessons.question: Explain why running both workloads through the same engine was the wrong simplification here, using what Hive and Impala are each actually architected to do well, and redesign which engine each workload should use.
lessons.solution:
-- ===== Workload 1: the nightly 5-year compliance rebuild -- HIVE fits =====
-- Hive's execution model (historically MapReduce, now commonly Tez or Spark
-- as the execution engine underneath HiveQL) is built around throughput over
-- large-scale, long-running batch jobs -- it tolerates and amortizes startup
-- and coordination overhead well because that overhead is small relative to
-- a 40-minute job touching years of data. Hive's cost-based optimizer and
-- its tolerance for very large, complex, multi-stage query plans (with
-- intermediate stages spilling to disk if needed) are exactly the properties
-- this batch job needs -- and Hive is *not* being used here because it is
-- "the safe default," but because a 40-minute, near-full-table batch job is
-- genuinely the workload Hive's execution model is built for.
CREATE TABLE compliance_report_2026 AS
SELECT
    c.customer_id, c.segment, c.risk_tier,
    COUNT(t.transaction_id)                     AS txn_count,
    SUM(t.amount)                                AS txn_total,
    MIN(t.transaction_date)                      AS earliest_txn,
    MAX(t.transaction_date)                      AS latest_txn
FROM iceberg_catalog.banking.transactions t
JOIN iceberg_catalog.banking.customer_dim c
    ON t.customer_id = c.customer_id
    AND t.transaction_date BETWEEN c.effective_from AND c.effective_to  -- point-in-time SCD2 join
WHERE t.transaction_date >= DATE '2021-08-21'
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.segment, c.risk_tier;

-- ===== Workload 2: ad-hoc, sub-5-second analyst lookups -- IMPALA fits =====
-- Impala uses its own MPP (massively parallel processing) execution engine,
-- with long-lived daemon processes on every node that skip the per-query
-- job-startup/coordination overhead a Hive-on-Tez/Spark job pays -- this is
-- the specific architectural reason Impala is built for low-latency,
-- interactive queries rather than Hive's throughput-oriented batch model.
-- Impala talks to the SAME Hive metastore and reads the SAME Iceberg
-- tables -- this is not a data duplication or a second copy of the data,
-- only a different, already-running execution engine pointed at it.
SELECT transaction_id, transaction_date, amount, merchant, status
FROM iceberg_catalog.banking.transactions
WHERE customer_id = 'CUST-2004471'
  AND transaction_date >= DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE(), INTERVAL 7 DAYS)
ORDER BY transaction_date DESC;
-- A filtered, partition-pruned lookup against one customer, one week --
-- exactly the shape of query Impala's daemon-based MPP engine answers in
-- low single-digit seconds, versus Hive's per-query job-startup overhead
-- dominating a query this small.
lessons.output:
Before (both workloads on Hive):
  Nightly compliance rebuild: ~40 min -- acceptable, matches Hive's design.
  Ad-hoc single-customer lookup: 20-40 sec -- almost entirely per-query
    job coordination/startup overhead, not actual data-scan time, because
    the query itself only touches a tiny, partition-pruned slice of data.

After (nightly rebuild on Hive, ad-hoc lookups on Impala):
  Nightly compliance rebuild: unchanged, ~40 min on Hive.
  Ad-hoc single-customer lookup: ~1-3 sec on Impala's always-running
    daemons -- same underlying Iceberg table, same Hive metastore,
    different execution engine matched to the query's actual latency need.
lessons.explanation:
**The junior engineer's "one engine is simpler" reasoning conflated operational simplicity with query-shape fitness -- and the two workloads in this scenario have genuinely different latency requirements that map onto genuinely different execution architectures, not just different tuning of the same engine.**

**Why Hive fits the nightly compliance rebuild:** Hive's execution model -- historically MapReduce, and in current Cloudera deployments typically Tez or Spark as the underlying execution engine for HiveQL -- is built around orchestrating large, multi-stage, often long-running jobs, with a cost-based optimizer suited to complex query plans over very large data volumes. The per-query overhead of planning and launching a job's execution stages is real, but it is small relative to a 40-minute job scanning years of transaction history -- this overhead is exactly what a throughput-oriented batch engine is designed to amortize, not eliminate.

**Why that same per-query overhead is what breaks the ad-hoc workload:** a query asking for one customer's transactions from the last week touches a tiny amount of actual data -- with correct partitioning, this is a fast scan. But when routed through Hive, the query still pays the same job-startup and coordination overhead a Hive job always pays, and for a query this small, that fixed overhead dominates the total response time. This is the concrete reason the analysts saw 20-40 second responses for a query that should complete in a couple of seconds: the bottleneck was never the amount of data scanned, it was the execution model's fixed per-query cost being applied to a workload shaped for a different execution model entirely.

**Why Impala is architected specifically to avoid that overhead:** Impala runs its own long-lived MPP (massively parallel processing) daemon on every relevant node in the cluster, continuously ready to execute queries without the job-submission and coordination steps a Hive-on-Tez/Spark job goes through for every single query. This is the specific mechanism behind Impala's interactive-latency positioning -- not a marketing claim, but a direct consequence of trading Hive's job-per-query model for always-running daemons that can start executing a query's fragments immediately.

**Why this required no data duplication or table redesign:** both engines, in a CDP deployment, read the same underlying Iceberg tables through the same Hive metastore (or Iceberg's own catalog layer built on top of it) -- routing the ad-hoc workload to Impala was purely a change in which execution engine a query goes through, not a data-copying or table-restructuring exercise. This is what makes "the right engine per workload shape" a genuinely low-cost fix once diagnosed correctly, versus the real cost of having initially misdiagnosed it as a configuration-tuning problem on a single engine.

**The general rule this generalizes to:** choosing between Hive and Impala (or, more broadly, between a throughput-oriented batch engine and an interactive MPP engine) should be driven by the query's actual latency requirement and data-touch pattern -- large-scan, latency-tolerant batch work fits Hive's job-oriented model; small, latency-sensitive, high-frequency lookups fit Impala's always-on daemon model -- not by a preference for operating fewer moving parts, which optimizes the wrong thing when the two workloads' actual requirements diverge this sharply.
lessons.readinessNote: The Hive/Impala engine-selection reasoning here assumes T01's storage-layer distinction (both engines here are reading Iceberg tables, which could sit on either HDFS or Ozone depending on the table) and feeds directly into T05's deeper look at how Iceberg's table format changes what both engines can do (time travel, schema evolution) without needing a data copy for either engine.

lessons.title: YARN and Cluster Resource Management
lessons.scenario: A shared CDP cluster runs three tenants: a nightly Spark ETL pipeline (large, bursty, tolerant of queueing), an always-on Spark Structured Streaming fraud-detection job (needs guaranteed, continuous resources, cannot tolerate being starved), and an ad-hoc data-science team running exploratory notebooks (unpredictable, low-priority, should never block the other two). All three currently submit to YARN's `default` queue with no further configuration. During a month-end batch spike, the fraud-detection streaming job is repeatedly starved of executors for several minutes at a time -- exactly the workload that was supposed to be guaranteed continuous resources -- while data-science notebook jobs continue running unaffected in the background.
lessons.question: Diagnose why submitting all three tenants to one undifferentiated queue caused the guaranteed-resource workload to be the one that got starved, and redesign the YARN capacity scheduler configuration so each tenant's actual resource requirement (guaranteed continuous, bursty-tolerant, low-priority-preemptible) is what YARN actually enforces.
lessons.solution:
<!-- capacity-scheduler.xml -- BEFORE: everything in one undifferentiated
     queue means YARN has no basis to distinguish "this job must never be
     starved" from "this job can wait." Within a single queue, YARN's
     scheduler allocates by submission order and configured per-queue
     policy, not by any notion of one specific application's business
     criticality -- so a burst of ETL applications can legitimately consume
     available containers before the streaming job's executors can be
     replaced or scaled, because nothing in the configuration told YARN
     the streaming job's resources were not to be touched. -->
<property>
  <name>yarn.scheduler.capacity.root.queues</name>
  <value>default</value>
</property>
<property>
  <name>yarn.scheduler.capacity.root.default.capacity</name>
  <value>100</value>
</property>

<!-- ===== AFTER: three queues, each matched to its tenant's real requirement ===== -->
<property>
  <name>yarn.scheduler.capacity.root.queues</name>
  <value>fraud_streaming,nightly_etl,data_science</value>
</property>

<!-- fraud_streaming: guaranteed capacity, minimal preemption risk --
     capacity + maximum-capacity pinned equal so it can never be squeezed
     below what it needs even under cluster-wide contention. -->
<property>
  <name>yarn.scheduler.capacity.root.fraud_streaming.capacity</name>
  <value>30</value>
</property>
<property>
  <name>yarn.scheduler.capacity.root.fraud_streaming.maximum-capacity</name>
  <value>30</value>
</property>
<!-- default-application-priority (NOT a bare "priority" property, which
     is not a real leaf-queue setting) sets the priority newly submitted
     applications in this queue get by default when they don't specify
     their own -- this affects ordering among applications already
     admitted to the queue, it is not what enforces the guaranteed
     capacity floor above. The floor is enforced by capacity ==
     maximum-capacity plus preemption, not by this property. -->
<property>
  <name>yarn.scheduler.capacity.root.fraud_streaming.default-application-priority</name>
  <value>10</value>
</property>

<!-- nightly_etl: a real guaranteed floor, but allowed to BURST above it
     into idle cluster capacity when other queues aren't using their share
     -- this is what "bursty-tolerant" means in capacity-scheduler terms:
     a generous maximum-capacity, but a modest guaranteed capacity so it
     cannot itself starve the other two queues when it bursts. -->
<property>
  <name>yarn.scheduler.capacity.root.nightly_etl.capacity</name>
  <value>50</value>
</property>
<property>
  <name>yarn.scheduler.capacity.root.nightly_etl.maximum-capacity</name>
  <value>80</value>
</property>

<!-- data_science: a small guaranteed floor, explicitly marked preemptible
     so YARN can reclaim its containers first when fraud_streaming or
     nightly_etl need capacity they are entitled to and are not getting. -->
<property>
  <name>yarn.scheduler.capacity.root.data_science.capacity</name>
  <value>20</value>
</property>
<property>
  <name>yarn.scheduler.capacity.root.data_science.maximum-capacity</name>
  <value>40</value>
</property>
<property>
  <name>yarn.scheduler.capacity.root.data_science.disable_preemption</name>
  <value>false</value>
</property>

<!-- Cluster-wide preemption must be ON for the above per-queue intent to
     actually be enforced -- without it, a queue below its guaranteed
     capacity has no mechanism to reclaim containers already granted to
     another queue, and the "guarantee" is only a target, not an
     enforced floor. -->
<property>
  <name>yarn.resourcemanager.scheduler.monitor.enable</name>
  <value>true</value>
</property>
lessons.output:
Before (one 'default' queue, no ACLs/preemption distinctions):
  Month-end ETL burst starves fraud_streaming's executors for several
  minutes at a time -- YARN has no configured basis to treat that job's
  resources as protected.

After (three capacity-scheduler queues + preemption enabled):
  fraud_streaming: guaranteed 30% capacity, capacity == maximum-capacity,
    so it can never be squeezed below its floor even during the ETL burst.
  nightly_etl: guaranteed 50%, can burst to 80% of cluster capacity when
    the other queues are idle -- but never at fraud_streaming's expense.
  data_science: guaranteed 20%, explicitly preemptible -- its containers
    are the first reclaimed if fraud_streaming or nightly_etl are below
    their guaranteed share and need capacity back.
lessons.explanation:
**The root cause was not "the cluster is too small" or "the fraud job needs more resources" -- it was that a single undifferentiated queue gives YARN no configuration-level information about which tenant's resource needs are actually non-negotiable, so YARN had nothing to enforce beyond first-come-first-served scheduling within that one queue.**

**Why one shared queue produced exactly this failure mode:** YARN's capacity scheduler allocates resources at the granularity of queues, using each queue's configured capacity and maximum-capacity to decide how contention is resolved. With all three tenants submitting to the single "default" queue, YARN has no per-tenant signal at all -- from its point of view, a burst of ETL applications and the fraud-detection streaming job's executor requests are indistinguishable competing demands on the same undifferentiated pool. During the month-end ETL burst, YARN simply granted containers to whichever applications requested them within that one queue's available capacity, with no configured basis to protect the streaming job's resources specifically -- which is exactly why the "supposedly guaranteed" workload was the one that got starved, while the genuinely low-priority data-science notebooks were unaffected (they were never competing hard for capacity in the first place, so the lack of differentiation happened not to hurt them this time).

**Why separate queues fix this, mechanically:** creating three queues with distinct capacity and maximum-capacity values gives YARN an actual configuration to enforce rather than relying on submission-order luck. Setting the fraud_streaming queue's capacity and maximum-capacity to the same value (30/30) is what makes its guarantee a hard floor rather than a soft target -- the queue can never be allocated less than its capacity when it has pending demand, and it is also capped there, which prevents it from ever needing to compete unpredictably for more. The nightly_etl queue's wider gap between capacity (50) and maximum-capacity (80) is what "bursty-tolerant" concretely means in capacity-scheduler terms: it can absorb a burst by using idle capacity beyond its guaranteed share, but only capacity the other queues are not currently using.

**Why preemption has to be explicitly enabled for any of this to matter under real contention:** capacity and maximum-capacity values are enforced going forward for new container requests, but if a queue is already below its guaranteed capacity because another queue's containers are occupying that capacity, YARN needs the scheduler's preemption monitor (yarn.resourcemanager.scheduler.monitor.enable) actively running to reclaim those containers back -- without it, a queue's "guarantee" is really only a target the scheduler tries to honor for new allocations, not an enforced floor it will actively restore once violated. This is precisely the mechanism that lets the data_science queue's containers be reclaimed first when fraud_streaming needs its guaranteed share back and is not getting it.

**The general resource-isolation principle this generalizes to:** shared-cluster resource contention needs to be modeled explicitly, per tenant, as a queue configuration with a real floor (capacity), a real ceiling (maximum-capacity), and an explicit preemption policy -- "everyone shares one pool and it works itself out" is not a resource-isolation strategy, it is the absence of one, and the specific tenant that suffers when contention actually happens is whichever one's requirement was never encoded into the scheduler's configuration in the first place.
lessons.readinessNote: This lesson's queue-based isolation model is the YARN-specific mechanism for exactly the same problem T04's discussion of container-based workload isolation (CDP's Kubernetes/OpenShift-based services) solves differently -- a learner who understands both is prepared for the real mixed estates T04 describes, where some workloads run under YARN's queue model and others under a container orchestrator's pod-level resource requests/limits, on the same platform.

lessons.title: Cloudera Data Platform Architecture
lessons.scenario: A new hire, who studied CDP entirely from a blog post describing 'the modern lakehouse platform,' joins a bank's data platform team expecting every workload to run as containerized microservices on Kubernetes with a single unified control plane. On their first day shadowing an incident, they watch a senior engineer diagnose a failed data-ingestion job by logging into Cloudera Manager's classic web UI, checking HDFS DataNode health and a YARN queue's pending-applications count -- none of which matches what the new hire expected to see. When they later ask why the team isn't 'just running everything on Kubernetes like the CDP docs describe,' the senior engineer explains that this specific cluster is CDP Private Cloud Base, and that Cloudera Manager-centric classic operations are still how most of this platform's day-to-day workloads are actually run.
lessons.question: Explain what CDP Private Cloud Base actually is architecturally, why 'CDP means Kubernetes-native microservices' is an overstatement of current reality even though CDP does have real container-based components, and where SDX fits into both the classic Cloudera-Manager-managed layer and any containerized services this platform might also run.
lessons.solution:
# --- What the senior engineer was actually looking at: classic Cloudera
# Manager-centric operations, which remain a real, current operational
# model many enterprise CDP Private Cloud Base clusters still run ---
# Cloudera Manager is CDP Private Cloud Base's central management plane:
# it manages service lifecycle (HDFS, YARN, Hive, Impala, Ozone, Kafka,
# etc.), health monitoring, configuration, and rolling upgrades across the
# cluster's hosts -- this is genuinely how a large share of real CDP
# estates are operated day to day, not a legacy interface being phased
# out from underneath the platform.

# Checking DataNode health via Cloudera Manager's underlying HDFS commands
# (what the senior engineer's diagnosis corresponds to at the CLI level):
hdfs dfsadmin -report | grep -A5 "Live datanodes"
yarn application -list -appStates RUNNING,ACCEPTED | grep "nightly-ingest"
yarn queue -status ingest_queue | grep -E "Pending Applications|Available"

# --- Where CDP genuinely IS container-based, and why that's not the whole
# platform ---
# CDP Private Cloud (the newer deployment model, distinct from Private
# Cloud Base) does run containerized data services -- Cloudera selected
# Red Hat OpenShift specifically as its container platform for this layer,
# giving CDP Private Cloud a genuinely Kubernetes-based architecture for
# the services deployed through it (e.g. Data Warehouse / CDW virtual
# warehouses, Machine Learning workspaces). This is real, current CDP
# architecture -- it is just not the same deployment as the classic
# Private Cloud Base cluster the senior engineer was diagnosing, and both
# models coexist across real enterprise estates rather than one having
# fully replaced the other.

oc get pods -n cdw-virtual-warehouse-fraud-analytics 2>/dev/null | head -5
# ^ this command would be relevant on a CDP Private Cloud (OpenShift-based)
# deployment's containerized Data Warehouse layer -- a genuinely different
# operational surface than the Cloudera-Manager-managed classic cluster
# the incident above was diagnosed on.

# --- Where SDX fits in EITHER case ---
# SDX (Shared Data Experience) is CDP's shared governance/security layer
# -- it is not itself a container platform or a classic-vs-modern
# distinction; it is meant to apply consistently across whichever compute
# layer is running the workload, so that security and governance policy
# is set once rather than per-service or per-deployment-model. Both the
# classic Cloudera-Manager-managed HDFS/YARN/Hive cluster and any
# OpenShift-based containerized CDW/ML workspace are meant to inherit the
# same SDX-governed policy -- this is the actual point of SDX existing as
# a distinct architectural layer rather than being folded into either
# deployment model specifically.
lessons.output:
New hire's mental model: "CDP = Kubernetes-native microservices,
  single unified control plane, Cloudera Manager is legacy."

What the senior engineer's incident diagnosis actually showed:
  CDP Private Cloud Base, Cloudera-Manager-centric operations, classic
  HDFS/YARN health checks -- a real, current, primary operational surface
  for this deployment model, not a phased-out legacy path.

The corrected picture: CDP Private Cloud Base (Cloudera Manager-centric,
  classic services) and CDP Private Cloud (OpenShift/Kubernetes-based
  containerized services like CDW virtual warehouses) are two distinct,
  coexisting deployment models -- SDX governance applies consistently
  across both, rather than "Kubernetes" describing the whole platform.
lessons.explanation:
**The new hire's mental model was built from marketing-oriented framing of CDP's newest capabilities, generalized into "this describes the whole platform" -- and the corrected picture matters because a data engineer who expects every CDP workload to be a Kubernetes microservice will misdiagnose or mishandle a real, current, classic-operations incident exactly the way this scenario sets up.**

**What CDP Private Cloud Base actually is:** it is Cloudera's on-premises deployment model built around the classic Hadoop-ecosystem services -- HDFS (and/or Ozone), YARN, Hive, Impala, Kafka, and others -- centrally managed through Cloudera Manager, which handles service lifecycle, health monitoring, configuration management, and rolling upgrades across the cluster's hosts. This is not a stripped-down or legacy-only deployment; it is a current, actively developed deployment model that many real enterprise estates still run day to day, not one being phased out in favor of container-based services. The senior engineer's incident diagnosis -- checking DataNode health via classic HDFS tooling and a YARN queue's pending-application count via Cloudera Manager -- is exactly what a real CDP Private Cloud Base operational workflow looks like, not an outdated way of doing things the platform has moved past.

**Where CDP genuinely does have container-based architecture, and why that doesn't contradict the above:** CDP Private Cloud (as a distinct deployment model from Private Cloud Base) does run services in containers, and Cloudera specifically selected Red Hat OpenShift as its container platform for this layer -- this gives CDP Private Cloud a real, current, Kubernetes-based architecture for the services deployed through it, such as Cloudera Data Warehouse's virtual warehouses or Machine Learning workspaces. The new hire's mistake was not believing containerized CDP components exist -- they genuinely do -- it was assuming this describes the entire platform uniformly, when in practice CDP Private Cloud Base's classic, Cloudera-Manager-centric model and CDP Private Cloud's OpenShift-based containerized model are two coexisting deployment options, and a real enterprise estate (like this bank's) may run either, or in practice often both across different parts of its data platform, rather than having fully migrated everything to one model.

**Where SDX fits into this, and why it's the layer that doesn't change between the two models:** SDX (Shared Data Experience) is CDP's shared security and governance layer -- it is explicitly designed to apply consistently regardless of which underlying compute/deployment model is running a given workload, so that access control, encryption, auditing, and metadata governance policy is defined once and enforced everywhere, rather than being redefined per-service or per-deployment-model. This is the architectural reason SDX exists as its own distinct layer in CDP's design rather than being bundled into either the classic Cloudera-Manager-managed services or the OpenShift-based containerized services specifically -- both are meant to sit underneath the same SDX-governed policy layer.

**The general lesson for someone learning CDP from current documentation and marketing material alike:** CDP's own official materials genuinely describe both a classic, Cloudera-Manager-centric operational reality and newer container-based services -- the risk is reading only the newest-feature-forward material and generalizing it into "this is how the whole platform works now," when a real production estate, like the one in this scenario, is very likely to include both models coexisting, with SDX as the one layer genuinely meant to be uniform across them.
lessons.readinessNote: T04's classic-vs-containerized distinction directly sets up T05 (which builds Iceberg's lakehouse story on top of either deployment model) and T06 (Kafka feeding Spark jobs that could themselves run under either YARN, on Private Cloud Base, or as OpenShift-orchestrated Spark-on-Kubernetes workloads on Private Cloud) -- a learner who collapses CDP into 'just Kubernetes' would misread which operational model either later lesson's examples actually assume.

lessons.title: Apache Iceberg and the Lakehouse on CDP
lessons.scenario: A bank's data-warehouse team is investigating why an Iceberg table's Hive metastore (HMS) partition-tracking has become a performance bottleneck as the fraud-analytics team added more and more date/region/channel partition combinations to a transactions table over eighteen months -- HMS calls for partition pruning during query planning are visibly slowing down, and DBAs are proposing to redesign HMS itself for more scale, assuming HMS partition-tracking is an unavoidable cost of using Hive-integrated tables. Separately, the compliance team wants to know whether they can query 'the transactions table exactly as it looked before last Tuesday's correction,' and initially assumes this would require a separate, manually-maintained backup table, since neither HDFS nor a traditional Hive table has a mechanism for that.
lessons.question: Explain, using Iceberg's actual catalog and snapshot mechanisms (not a generic 'Iceberg makes everything better' claim), why the HMS partition-tracking bottleneck is specifically an artifact of how Iceberg tables integrate with Hive rather than an unavoidable Hive cost, and why the compliance team's time-travel requirement needs no separate backup table at all.
lessons.solution:
-- ===== The HMS partition-pressure diagnosis =====
-- In a CLASSIC (non-Iceberg) Hive table, partition metadata -- which
-- partitions exist, their locations, their statistics -- is tracked
-- directly inside the Hive metastore's relational database, and grows
-- with every distinct partition combination. This is a real, well-known
-- HMS scaling cost for highly-partitioned classic Hive tables.

-- An ICEBERG table changes this specifically: partition (and file-level)
-- metadata lives in Iceberg's own metadata files on the file system /
-- object store -- manifest lists and manifest files -- NOT primarily
-- inside HMS's relational tables. By default, Hive and Impala access
-- Iceberg tables through Iceberg's HiveCatalog, which uses HMS mainly to
-- store a POINTER to the table's current Iceberg metadata location, not
-- the full partition-by-partition detail HMS tracks for classic tables.
DESCRIBE FORMATTED iceberg_catalog.banking.transactions;
-- ^ shows the HMS entry is a thin pointer to Iceberg table metadata,
-- not a full per-partition catalog the way a classic Hive table's HMS
-- entry would be.

-- If the DBAs' bottleneck is showing up as slow HMS calls during
-- partition pruning, that is the signal the table (or the query engine's
-- configuration) may still be going through a classic-Hive-style
-- partition-discovery path rather than Iceberg's own manifest-based
-- pruning -- the actual fix is confirming and correcting THAT, not
-- scaling HMS itself for a cost Iceberg tables were specifically
-- designed to relieve HMS of.
SELECT * FROM iceberg_catalog.banking.transactions
WHERE txn_date = DATE '2026-08-14' AND region = 'MENA' AND channel = 'mobile';
-- Iceberg's own manifest files let the query engine prune to exactly the
-- relevant data files using Iceberg's metadata layer directly, without
-- needing HMS to enumerate every partition combination the way a classic
-- Hive table's partition-pruning would.

-- ===== The compliance team's time-travel requirement =====
-- No separate backup table is needed: every write to an Iceberg table
-- (insert, MERGE, overwrite) produces a new, immutable SNAPSHOT recorded
-- in the table's metadata -- prior snapshots are retained (until an
-- explicit expiration/cleanup policy removes them), which is what makes
-- time travel a built-in property of the table format, not a manually
-- maintained parallel structure.
SELECT snapshot_id, committed_at, operation
FROM iceberg_catalog.banking.transactions.snapshots
ORDER BY committed_at DESC
LIMIT 5;

SELECT *
FROM iceberg_catalog.banking.transactions
FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF '2026-08-18 23:59:59'  -- the moment before last Tuesday's correction
WHERE customer_id = 'CUST-2004471';
-- Reads the table exactly as its committed snapshot state was at that
-- timestamp -- the correction's effect is simply not visible in that
-- older snapshot, with no separate backup table, restore process, or
-- manual versioning scheme required.

  partition explicitly -- cost genuinely grows with partition count.
  This Iceberg table (via HiveCatalog): HMS holds a pointer to Iceberg
  metadata; partition/file-level pruning is meant to happen through
  Iceberg's own manifest files. Slow HMS calls during pruning indicate
  the query path is not using Iceberg's manifest-based pruning as
  designed -- not that HMS itself needs to be re-architected for scale.

Compliance time-travel query:

lessons.explanation:
**Both parts of this scenario share one root cause for the confusion: treating Iceberg as "a Hive table with extra features" rather than understanding that Iceberg specifically relocates certain responsibilities away from HMS and Hive's classic model, onto its own metadata and snapshot mechanisms.**

**Why the HMS partition-pressure bottleneck is an Iceberg-integration artifact, not an unavoidable Hive cost:** a classic (non-Iceberg) Hive table genuinely does track partition metadata inside HMS's own relational database -- adding more partition combinations over time genuinely does grow HMS's relational metadata and genuinely can become a real scaling bottleneck, which is exactly the assumption the DBAs brought to this investigation. Iceberg tables are architected differently on purpose: partition and data-file metadata lives in Iceberg's own manifest lists and manifest files, stored alongside the table's data, not primarily inside HMS's relational schema. When Hive or Impala access an Iceberg table through Iceberg's HiveCatalog (the default catalog implementation), HMS's role narrows to holding a pointer to the table's current Iceberg metadata location -- the actual partition-pruning and file-selection work is meant to happen by reading Iceberg's own manifest files directly, which is specifically what relieves HMS of the partition-count-driven scaling cost a classic Hive table would carry. If the DBAs are seeing HMS calls slow down specifically during partition pruning on an Iceberg table, the correct diagnosis is that something in the query path is not using Iceberg's manifest-based pruning as designed (a misconfigured catalog, an engine falling back to a classic-Hive-style partition-enumeration path) -- not that HMS itself has hit an unavoidable Iceberg-table scaling limit that requires re-architecting HMS.

**Why the compliance team's time-travel need requires no separate backup table:** every write to an Iceberg table -- an insert, a MERGE, an overwrite, a correction -- produces a new, immutable snapshot, recorded in the table's own metadata history. Prior snapshots remain queryable (until an explicit retention/expiration policy removes them) precisely because Iceberg's commit model is snapshot-based rather than being a simple "current state only" pointer the way a classic table effectively is. Querying "the table as it looked before last Tuesday's correction" is therefore not a request that needs a parallel backup structure at all -- it is a direct read against an older snapshot the table format already retained as part of doing its normal writes. This is the same underlying snapshot mechanism Chapter 3's lakehouse lesson (Data Lake vs. Data Warehouse vs. Lakehouse) established as what makes an Iceberg write atomic and crash-safe -- time travel and atomic commits are two consequences of the same snapshot-history design, not two separate features.

**The general principle that connects both halves of this lesson:** understanding what specifically changed when a table moved from "classic Hive table" to "Iceberg table accessed via Hive/Impala" -- which metadata now lives where, and which capabilities that relocation newly makes possible -- is what lets an engineer correctly attribute a bottleneck or newly-available capability to its real cause, rather than either assuming Iceberg tables inherit every classic-Hive limitation unchanged, or assuming "Iceberg" is a vague synonym for "better" without a specific mechanism behind the improvement.

lessons.title: Kafka for Enterprise Event Streaming
lessons.scenario: A bank's card-authorization event pipeline publishes every swipe to a Kafka topic with 12 partitions, keyed by `card_id`, consumed by a fraud-scoring Spark Structured Streaming job running with a consumer group of 4 instances for parallelism. During a Black Friday-style volume spike, the platform team notices something specific: 3 of the 4 consumer instances are running near-idle while the 4th is falling further and further behind, its consumer lag climbing into the millions of events, even though the topic overall has plenty of partitions and the consumer group has capacity. A separate concern surfaces the same week: a different team wants to replay the last 24 hours of card-authorization events into a newly-deployed version of the fraud model for backtesting, without disrupting the live fraud-scoring consumer group at all.
lessons.question: Diagnose why keying by `card_id` produced this specific lopsided-consumer-lag pattern rather than an even spread across the 4 consumer instances, and explain the Kafka mechanism (not a vague 'add more partitions') that lets the replay team read the last 24 hours without touching the live consumer group's state at all.
lessons.solution:
from kafka import KafkaConsumer, TopicPartition
from kafka.admin import KafkaAdminClient

# --- Diagnosing the lopsided consumer lag ---
# Kafka guarantees ORDERING per partition, not per topic -- and a topic's
# partition assignment for a keyed message is a deterministic function of
# the key (by default, a hash of the key modulo partition count). Every
# event for the SAME card_id always lands on the SAME partition, which is
# what preserves per-card event ordering -- but it also means partition
# load is only as balanced as the KEY distribution actually is, not
# guaranteed even just because there are 12 partitions and 4 consumers.

admin = KafkaAdminClient(bootstrap_servers="broker1:9092,broker2:9092")
consumer = KafkaConsumer(bootstrap_servers="broker1:9092,broker2:9092",
                          group_id="fraud-scoring-group")

partitions = [TopicPartition("card-authorizations", p) for p in range(12)]
consumer.assign(partitions)
end_offsets = consumer.end_offsets(partitions)
committed = {p: consumer.committed(p) for p in partitions}
for p in partitions:
    lag = end_offsets[p] - (committed[p] or 0)
    print(f"partition {p.partition}: lag={lag}")
# If this shows lag concentrated on a small number of partitions (not
# spread evenly across all 12), the root cause is almost certainly key
# skew: a small number of high-volume card_ids (e.g. a small set of
# corporate/high-frequency merchant-facing cards during a Black-Friday-
# style spike) hashing onto the same one or two partitions, and those
# specific partitions' assigned consumer instance falling behind while
# the other partitions -- and the consumer instances handling them --
# stay comfortably caught up. Adding partitions alone would not fix this:
# the same skewed keys would still hash onto a proportionally smaller
# but still-skewed subset of a larger partition count, unless the
# partitioning key itself changes.

# A real fix needs to address the SKEW, not just the partition count --
# e.g. a composite key (card_id + a time-bucket salt) for very
# high-volume cards specifically, while preserving per-card ordering
# within each time bucket, which is enough for fraud-scoring's actual
# ordering requirement (recent-window pattern detection, not
# all-time-ever ordering per card).

# --- The replay-without-disrupting-the-live-consumer-group requirement ---
# Kafka retains events in a topic for its configured retention period
# (independent of whether any consumer group has read them), and
# consumer OFFSETS are tracked per consumer GROUP -- this is the
# mechanism that makes replay-without-disruption possible: a second,
# independent consumer group reading the same topic has its own,
# completely separate offset tracking from the live fraud-scoring group's.
replay_consumer = KafkaConsumer(
    bootstrap_servers="broker1:9092,broker2:9092",
    group_id="fraud-backtest-replay-group",   # a DIFFERENT consumer group
    auto_offset_reset="earliest",
)
replay_partitions = [TopicPartition("card-authorizations", p) for p in range(12)]
replay_consumer.assign(replay_partitions)

import time
target_ts = int((time.time() - 24 * 3600) * 1000)  # 24 hours ago, in ms
offsets_for_times = replay_consumer.offsets_for_times(
    {p: target_ts for p in replay_partitions}
)
for p, offset_and_ts in offsets_for_times.items():
    if offset_and_ts is not None:
        replay_consumer.seek(p, offset_and_ts.offset)
# The replay group now reads from 24 hours ago, at its own pace, against
# its own offsets -- the live fraud-scoring group's partition assignment,
# committed offsets, and processing rate are completely untouched by
# this, because Kafka tracks progress per (topic, partition, consumer
# GROUP), not once per topic globally.

Consumer-lag diagnosis (per-partition):
  partitions 0-8, 10-11: lag in the low hundreds -- healthy.
  partition 9: lag climbing into the millions -- this single partition,
    assigned to one of the 4 consumer instances, is where a
    disproportionate share of card_ids hashed during the spike.

Root cause: key skew (a small number of very high-volume card_ids
  hashing onto the same partition), not insufficient partition count or
  insufficient consumer parallelism -- the other 3 instances have spare
  capacity precisely because their assigned partitions never saw the
  same concentration of high-volume keys.

Replay: a second consumer group ("fraud-backtest-replay-group") reads

  the live "fraud-scoring-group"'s committed offsets and consumption
  rate -- confirmed via each group's own, separately-tracked lag.
lessons.explanation:
**Both halves of this scenario turn on the same underlying Kafka mechanism -- partition assignment and offset tracking are both scoped more narrowly than "the topic," and understanding exactly what they're scoped to (the partition, and the consumer group, respectively) is what explains both the skew problem and the replay solution.**

**Why keying by card_id produced lopsided lag rather than an even 4-way split:** Kafka's ordering guarantee is per-partition, not per-topic -- to preserve the order of events for a given key (here, all of one card's authorization events, which fraud-scoring genuinely needs in order to detect patterns like rapid repeated swipes), every event with the same key must be routed to the same partition, deterministically, typically via a hash of the key modulo the partition count. This is a real, necessary property for the fraud-scoring use case, not an implementation detail that could simply be turned off -- but it has a direct consequence: partition load balance is only as good as the actual distribution of key values feeding it. If a small number of card_ids generate a disproportionate share of events during a volume spike (a plausible real pattern -- certain corporate or merchant-facing cards see much higher authorization frequency than typical retail cards, and a Black-Friday-style spike would concentrate exactly this kind of activity), those specific card_ids' events all land on the same one or two partitions regardless of how many total partitions or consumer instances exist. The consumer instance assigned to that specific partition falls behind while the other three, whose assigned partitions never saw the same concentration, stay comfortably caught up -- which is exactly the lopsided pattern observed, and precisely why "add more partitions" would not fix it: a larger partition count changes the modulus in the hash, but the same skewed keys still concentrate onto whichever subset of the larger partition count they now hash to, unless the actual partitioning key changes to something with less skew (e.g. a composite key that distributes high-volume cards' events across multiple partitions using a bounded time-bucket salt, while still preserving the ordering fraud-scoring actually needs within each bucket).

**Why the replay team can read the last 24 hours without touching the live consumer group at all:** Kafka's two independent scoping mechanisms are what make this possible. First, a topic retains its events for its configured retention period regardless of whether any particular consumer group has read them yet -- reading is non-destructive, so the live fraud-scoring group consuming the topic does not remove or consume the data away from any other reader. Second, and more directly relevant here, consumer *offsets* -- the bookkeeping of "how far has this reader gotten" -- are tracked per (topic, partition, consumer **group**), not once globally per topic. A second consumer group, with its own group id, has entirely separate offset state from the live group's; seeking that second group's offsets back to a timestamp 24 hours in the past (via offsets_for_times, which maps a timestamp to the earliest offset at or after it) only affects that new group's own bookkeeping. The live fraud-scoring group's committed offsets, partition assignment, and processing rate are untouched, because nothing about the replay group's operations writes to or reads from the live group's own tracked state.

**The general principle both halves illustrate:** Kafka's core guarantees (ordering, offset tracking) are deliberately scoped narrower than "the topic as a whole" -- ordering is per-partition, offsets are per-group-per-partition -- and treating either as if it applied topic-wide (assuming "12 partitions means load spreads evenly" or worrying "another reader might disrupt the live consumers") is the specific misunderstanding this lesson's two problems are each built to correct.
